694.title: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening
694.hook: four teachers are asked what bhakti looks like, and the book lets every one of them answer
694.howItsDone: In many Vaishnava homes and temples, devotion takes all four shapes the sutras name: daily puja, retelling and singing the stories of Krishna or Rama, quiet remembrance, and offering one's work to God. Groups often study a few sutras at a time with a teacher's commentary.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and the opening of the Narada Bhakti Sutras. Now, then, we will explain bhakti; and the definition, supreme love. Which love did you catch yourself meaning? Day six hundred ninety-four.

Ask four people who love someone how you can tell, and you'll get four answers. One says: they show up. One says: they can't stop talking about them. One says: they're just happy. And one says: watch what happens when they're apart. The Narada Bhakti Sutras do something like that. A little way into the book, having defined bhakti as supreme love, they stop and ask: but what are its marks? And instead of one answer, they let four teachers speak.
screen: `HOW CAN YOU TELL SOMEONE LOVES?` → `FOUR PEOPLE, FOUR ANSWERS.` → `THE SUTRAS ASK THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Sutra fifteen sets it up: now its marks are described, according to different views. First, Vyasa, the son of Parashara, the sage tradition credits with the Mahabharata. For him, bhakti is fondness for worship: the lamp, the flowers, the offering. Second, Garga. For him, it's fondness for talk about the Lord: the stories, told and retold. Third, Shandilya. For him, it's delight in the Self that nothing gets in the way of. Three teachers, three marks, and the text doesn't call any of them wrong. Then sutra nineteen gives Narada's own view. Bhakti is offering every action to the Lord, and feeling the deepest anguish on forgetting him. The word there is vyakulata: being thrown into turmoil, unsettled, like someone who's lost a child in a crowd. It's a striking definition. Love is measured not only by what you do, but by how much it hurts to forget. Then the sutras give an example: it is like the cowherd women of Vraja, the gopis, who loved Krishna. And they head off a misreading. Even the gopis, the text says, did not forget his greatness. Love without that, it says, would be like the love of a secret lover, who takes no joy in the beloved's joy. So here, at its opening, a short book on devotion makes room for several teachers before it speaks for itself. Four marks, then: the lamp and flowers, the stories, the quiet joy, and the ache. The book keeps all four.
screen: `VYASA: FONDNESS FOR WORSHIP.` · `GARGA: LOVE OF THE STORIES.` · `SHANDILYA: DELIGHT IN THE SELF.` · `NARADA: ANGUISH ON FORGETTING.` · then, large: `LIKE THE GOPIS OF VRAJA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring back what you love most, the one from yesterday. Now try each teacher's mark, lightly. Is there something you do for it, a small act of care? Is there a story about it you love to tell? Is there a plain gladness, just that it exists? And if it slipped out of your mind for a whole day, would you feel the gap? No answer is the right one. Let them come, and then just breathe. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion. Vyasa sees it in worship, Garga in the stories, Shandilya in delight, and Narada in the ache of forgetting.
Your line: the ache of forgetting. Today, offer one ordinary action, a meal, a reply, a walk, to what you love, and notice if you forget. Day six hundred ninety-four.

options: offering every act, and anguish on forgetting.

fork.reveal: sutra nineteen: offering all actions to him, and the deepest anguish on forgetting him. love measured by the ache of the gap.

what it means: the sutras let four teachers name its marks: worship, the stories, delight, and the ache of forgetting.

695.title: jnana — Shankara's *Atmabodha*
695.hook: a short Sanskrit poem says action can't remove ignorance, any more than sweeping can remove the dark
695.carry: light, not sweeping, ends the dark
695.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta circles, the Atmabodha is often among the first texts a student reads with a teacher, verse by verse, alongside listening, reflection and meditation on the teaching. Students often combine study like this with work done as service and with devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and four teachers in the Narada Bhakti Sutras: worship, the stories, delight, and Narada's own, the ache of forgetting. Did you offer one ordinary action? Day six hundred ninety-five.

A dark room, at night. You could sweep it. You could scrub the floor, rearrange the furniture, work there all night. None of it removes the dark. One thing does, and it takes no effort at all: the light. That picture sits near the beginning of a short Sanskrit poem called the Atmabodha, knowledge of the Self, which tradition gives to Shankara. Today the third strand of this lineage track: after karma, the path of action, and bhakti, the path of love, jnana, the path of knowing.
screen: `A DARK ROOM.` → `SWEEPING WON'T HELP.` → `THE THIRD STRAND: JNANA.`

segments.voice: The Atmabodha is short, a kind of pocket handbook of Advaita Vedanta, the teaching that the Self and Brahman are not two. Tradition credits it to Shankara; some scholars question whether he wrote it, and it's often studied as a beginner's text. The first verse says who it's for: people whose faults have been worn down by discipline, who are calm, free of craving, and long for freedom. So it starts where the karma days left off: a disciplined life has already prepared the mind. Then the second verse makes its claim. Just as fire is what actually cooks the food, the poem says, knowledge, not any other practice, is what directly brings liberation. Verse three gives the reason. Action isn't opposed to ignorance, so action can't destroy it. Knowledge is opposed to it, the way light is opposed to darkness. And verse four: because of ignorance, the Self seems limited; when ignorance goes, the Self shines on its own, like the sun when the clouds pass. The word jnana means knowing, from the root jna, to know. But it doesn't mean collecting facts. It's closer to the moment you see that the thing you feared was never there. Here the schools of Vedanta take different roads. Shankara's school holds that knowledge alone liberates, and that action and devotion ready the mind for it. Teachers in Ramanuja's tradition hold that devotion to the Lord, supported by knowledge, is the way. Both are living Hindu paths, each with its own teachers, temples and students reading verse by verse.
screen: `FOR THE CALM WHO LONG TO BE FREE.` · `FIRE COOKS; KNOWLEDGE FREES.` · `LIGHT, NOT SWEEPING, ENDS THE DARK.` · `THE SUN BEHIND THE CLOUDS.` · then, large: `JNANA: KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Sit still and let the breath be easy. Notice something simple: you're aware. Sounds come and go, and you're aware of them. Thoughts come and go, and you're aware of them. Feelings in the body come and go. Don't chase any of them. Just rest as the one who notices, the way the sky stays while the clouds cross it. If you drift, that's fine; noticing the drift is the practice too. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing, from the root to know. In the Atmabodha, the light that ends the dark of ignorance.
Your line: light, not sweeping, ends the dark. Today, when a worry looms, ask once: is this a snake, or just a shadow I haven't put the light on? Day six hundred ninety-five.

trapdoor: what you thought: jnana means book learning.
what it means: it's knowing the Self directly, the light that ends ignorance.

696.title: Year two close
696.hook: three hundred sixty-five sessions: seven Upanishads, the Yoga Sutras, the whole Ramayana, a year of festivals, and three paths
696.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
696.howItsDone: Hindus often mark the end of a course of study, or the completion of a text, with a closing recitation, a peace chant, and an offering of thanks to the teacher. Some families sponsor a reading or feed guests when a long recitation is finished.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jnana, and Shankara's Atmabodha. Sweeping won't clear a dark room; only the light does. Was there a shadow you put the light on? Today, the last day of year two. Day six hundred ninety-six.

Three hundred sixty-five sessions ago, year two opened with a promise: the texts underneath. Not the stories people tell about Hinduism, but the old pages the stories rest on. Since then you've sat with a father telling his son, that you are. You've read a sage defining yoga in one short line. You've walked the whole Ramayana, from a bird's cry to the earth opening. You've kept a year of festivals. Today we stand at the top and look back down the slope.
screen: `THE TEXTS UNDERNEATH.` → `THREE HUNDRED SIXTY-FIVE SESSIONS.` → `LOOK BACK DOWN THE SLOPE.`

segments.voice: Four blocks. First, the seven big Upanishads: the Chandogya, the Brihadaranyaka, the Taittiriya, the Aitareya, the Prashna, the Mundaka and the Shvetashvatara. Uddalaka and the salt in the water, and his line to Shvetaketu, tat tvam asi, that you are. Gargi asking her questions like arrows. The two kinds of knowledge. Second, the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, in four parts, opening with atha, now, and then the definition: yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Third, Valmiki's Ramayana, seven books in a hundred and eighty sessions: a bow broken, sandals on a throne, a leap across the sea, a homecoming, and a later book whose ending the tradition still argues over with love. Fourth, the festival year, from Janmashtami's midnight to Shivaratri's all-night watch, and then the three strands of the lineage track. Karma, with the Isha asking the mind to remember what was done. Bhakti, with Narada's supreme love and the ache of forgetting. Jnana, with Shankara's light in the dark room. Why call it the summit of the texts? Because so much of what comes next leans on these pages. Later teachers keep returning to the Upanishads. Yoga teachers still go back to Patanjali's sutras. Poets retold Valmiki in other tongues: Kamban in Tamil, Tulsidas in Awadhi. Hindus don't all read these texts the same way, and the schools you met this week read them differently. But they read the same roots. Tomorrow, year three begins with the Mahabharata, and it opens not with a battle but with a king and a sacrifice of snakes.
screen: `SEVEN UPANISHADS: THAT YOU ARE.` · `PATANJALI: STILLING THE MIND.` · `VALMIKI: SEVEN BOOKS.` · `FESTIVALS, AND THREE PATHS.` · then, large: `YOU'VE READ THE ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Sit as if at the top of a hill, the whole year below you. Let one line from year two rise on its own: that you are, or the stilling of the mind, or remember what was done, or anything else that stayed. Don't choose; wait for it. When it comes, hold it in the breath, in on the first half, out on the second. Then let it rest, and just look out over the year. The bell holds the time.
Mula. The root: seven Upanishads, the Yoga Sutras, the Ramayana, the festival year, and three paths, all read at the source later teachers keep returning to.
Your line: you've read the roots. Today, tell one person one thing from year two that surprised you. Day six hundred ninety-six, and year two is done.

screen: `DAY 696 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ADI PARVA: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE FRAME.`

697.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
697.hook: a traveler walks into a forest of sages and says he's come from a king's snake sacrifice, where he heard the whole story
697.carry: a story told beside a fire
697.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
697.howItsDone: In some Hindu homes and temples the Mahabharata is read or recited in parts over many days, with a reciter retelling and explaining each section to listeners. This year follows Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English translation, which is in the public domain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day of year two: mula, the root. Your line was you've read the roots. Who did you tell? Today, year three begins. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

A forest called Naimisha. The sages of Shaunaka are keeping a long sacrifice there, and between the rites they have time to listen. A traveler arrives: Ugrashravas, known as Sauti, the son of the storyteller Lomaharshana. They make him welcome, and they ask what anyone asks a visitor: where have you come from? He has come, he says, from the snake sacrifice of King Janamejaya. There he heard a great story told from beginning to end. The sages want all of it. So year three opens the way the Mahabharata opens: not on a battlefield, but in a forest, with someone asking for a story.
screen: `A FOREST, A SACRIFICE, A VISITOR.` → `WHERE HAVE YOU COME FROM?` → `A STORY HEARD AT A KING'S FIRE.`

segments.voice: This is the Adi Parva, the opening book of the Mahabharata. This year we read the Mahabharata as a serial, a piece at a time, following Kisari Mohan Ganguli's English. And before we meet a single hero, the Adi Parva builds a frame. Here's how it nests. In the forest, Sauti tells the sages what he heard. What he heard was told at King Janamejaya's sacrifice by Vaishampayana, a disciple of Vyasa. And Vyasa, the text says, is the one who composed the poem in the first place. So the story reaches us hand to hand: Vyasa to his disciple, the disciple to a king, the king's hall to a traveler, the traveler to a forest of sages, and now, through the book, to you. Who is this king? Janamejaya comes from the line of the Pandavas, the heroes of the war to come. His father, King Parikshit, died from the bite of Takshaka, a king of the snakes. And Janamejaya answered with a great fire sacrifice meant to draw the snakes into the flames. It's at that sacrifice that the story of his own ancestors is told. Hold that picture, because the whole poem sits inside it. A grieving son, a fire built for revenge, and beside the fire, someone telling him how his family's war began. Some readers hear the frame as a question the poem puts to itself from its first pages: what does a man in the middle of vengeance need to hear? Over the next days we'll walk the frame slowly: a pair of stolen earrings, a snake who speaks for mercy, a bet over a horse's tail, a bird who steals the nectar of the gods, a curse on a king, and a young sage who asks for the fire to stop. Then the story proper begins.
screen: `THE OPENING BOOK.` · `A STORY PASSED HAND TO HAND.` · `A KING'S FATHER, A SNAKE'S BITE.` · `A FIRE BUILT FOR REVENGE.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE POEM SITS INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down. Notice the circles you're sitting in. First, the breath itself, going in and out. Then the body around it. Then the room and its sounds. Then, wider, the people who handed you the stories you live by: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend at a kitchen table. Let one face come. You don't have to do anything with it. Just let that person sit at the edge of the circle while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Adi Parva. The opening book of the Mahabharata, where the whole story is told beside a king's snake sacrifice.
Your line: a story told beside a fire. Today, when someone tells you a story, ask once where they heard it. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

screen: `DAY 697 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ADI PARVA: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE FRAME.`

698.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
698.hook: a student loses a queen's earrings to a disguised snake king, and carries the grudge all the way to Janamejaya
698.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
698.howItsDone: Paying a teacher's fee at the end of study, guru dakshina, is a custom some Hindu students still keep, often as a gift or a service the teacher asks for. In the Adi Parva, Uttanka's journey ends at Janamejaya's court, and that is where the snake sacrifice begins to be urged.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Adi Parva opened in a forest: a traveler, and a story first told at King Janamejaya's snake sacrifice. Whose story did you trace back? Day six hundred ninety-eight.

A student finishes his studies and asks his teacher what fee he can pay. The teacher sends him to ask his wife, and she names it: the earrings worn by the queen of King Paushya, brought back in time for a rite she means to wear them to. The student's name is Uttanka. He goes, and the queen gives him the earrings, with a warning: Takshaka, the king of the snakes, wants them badly. Be careful. On the road home, Uttanka sets the earrings down to wash before his prayers. When he looks up, they're gone. Today's piece of the frame is how a snake king made an enemy.
screen: `A STUDENT'S FEE.` → `A QUEEN'S EARRINGS.` → `SET DOWN, AND GONE.`

segments.voice: The thief was a wandering beggar, and as Uttanka chases him, the beggar drops the disguise. It's Takshaka. He slips into a hole in the earth, down into the world of the snakes, and Uttanka follows him. What happens down there reads like a dream. Uttanka praises the snakes in verses, and still doesn't get the earrings back. He sees two women at a loom, weaving with black and white threads. He sees a wheel turned by boys, and a man with a horse. The man tells him to blow into the horse, and when he does, smoke and fire pour through the snake world, and a frightened Takshaka hands the earrings back. When Uttanka gets home, his teacher explains the figures he saw as gods and powers; the horse, he says, was Agni, fire itself. Uttanka pays his fee in time. Done, you'd think. But Uttanka doesn't let it go. He travels to the capital, to King Janamejaya, and tells the king: Takshaka is the one who killed your father. Avenge him. Now look at what the Adi Parva is doing. The snake sacrifice doesn't begin with the king's grief alone. It begins with a student's grudge, carried a long way and set beside someone else's wound. Uttanka has his own score with Takshaka, and he finds a king with a bigger one. That's a question the frame keeps raising: how does anger spread? Not always from the person who was hurt. Sometimes from the one standing next to them, saying, you shouldn't let this go. Janamejaya turns to his ministers and asks how his father died. Their answer comes in a few days. First, the frame turns aside, and a snake speaks up for mercy.
screen: `THE BEGGAR WAS TAKSHAKA.` · `DOWN INTO THE SNAKE WORLD.` · `SMOKE AND FIRE; THE EARRINGS BACK.` · `UTTANKA GOES TO THE KING.` · then, large: `HOW DOES ANGER SPREAD?`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a grudge you've been handed. Not one that began with you: one someone else passed you. A family feud. A coworker's complaint about someone you barely know. An old story about a whole group of people. Just notice it, set down in front of you, the way Uttanka set the earrings on the ground. Whose was it first? Did you choose to carry it? You don't have to put it down today. Just see it clearly for a minute, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where a student's grudge against a snake king reaches a king's ear.
Your line: how does anger spread? Today, when someone hands you their anger, notice it before you pick it up. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

screen: `DAY 698 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ADI PARVA: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE FRAME.`

699.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
699.hook: a grieving groom vows to kill every snake he meets, until a harmless one speaks up and teaches him not to harm
699.carry: we share the name, nothing else
699.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
699.howItsDone: Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is taught in Hindu texts beyond this one, and some Hindus practice it through vegetarian diet, care for animals, and restraint in speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Adi Parva: Uttanka, the stolen earrings, and a grudge carried all the way to King Janamejaya. Did someone hand you their anger? Day six hundred ninety-nine.

The wedding has been set. The bride, Pramadvara, is out with her friends, and she steps on a snake she doesn't see. It bites her, and she dies. The groom is Ruru, a young man of the family of the sage Bhrigu. He goes off alone into the forest and weeps. Then a messenger of the gods comes to him with an offer: she can live again, if he gives her half of his own life. He gives it. She wakes. They marry. It could end there, happily. It doesn't.
screen: `A BRIDE, A HIDDEN SNAKE.` → `HALF HIS LIFE FOR HERS.` → `IT DOESN'T END THERE.`

segments.voice: Ruru makes a vow. From now on, whenever he sees a snake, he will kill it. And he keeps the vow. He carries a heavy stick, and he strikes the snakes he finds. One day he comes on an old snake lying on the ground, of a kind called a dundubha, and he raises the stick. The snake speaks. I've done you no harm, it says. Why strike me? Ruru answers that a snake killed his wife, so he kills snakes. The dundubha answers: we're not the ones who bite. We share the name snake with them, and nothing else. Then it tells Ruru who it really is: a sage, cursed to live in this shape until the day it met him. Standing as a man again, the sage gives Ruru a teaching. Not harming living beings, he says, is the highest dharma. A man of a priestly family should be known for gentleness and forgiveness, not for the stick. Notice where the Adi Parva puts this. We're inside the frame of a king trying to burn the snakes. And before we get to that fire, the poem lets a creature in a snake's shape speak for ahimsa, not harming. Ruru's grief was real. His rage was real. But he had turned one bite into a war on a whole kind of creature. The sage even points ahead: he mentions Janamejaya's snake sacrifice, and that it was stopped. Then he's gone. Ruru goes home and asks his father to tell him the rest. And that's how the poem gets us back to the fire: a grieving man, freshly taught mercy, asking how a king's war on the snakes began and ended.
screen: `RURU'S VOW: KILL EVERY SNAKE.` · `WE'RE NOT THE ONES WHO BITE.` · `A SAGE UNDER A CURSE.` · `NOT HARMING: THE HIGHEST DHARMA.` · then, large: `AHIMSA.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go on its own for a moment. Bring to mind one hurt that came from one person, or one thing. Now notice whether it has spread: from one dog to all dogs, one driver to all drivers, one person to everyone who looks like them. Don't argue with it. 700.howItsDone: In some regions Hindu families honor snakes, nagas, at the festival of Nag Panchami. In the Adi Parva, Kadru's curse is the snakes' own family story: why the fire was coming for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Adi Parva: Ruru's stick, and a harmless snake who taught him not to harm. Did one bad experience try to speak for a whole group? Day seven hundred.

What color is a white horse's tail? That's the bet between two sisters. They're both wives of the sage Kashyapa, Kadru and Vinata, and they've just seen a marvelous white horse, Uchchaihshravas, which rose from the churning of the ocean. Vinata says the horse is white all over. Kadru says no: its tail is black. They make it a wager, and the stakes are steep: the loser becomes the winner's slave. They agree to go and look. Before they do, Kadru calls her sons. Her sons are snakes. Today we reach the root of the snake sacrifice.
screen: `A WHITE HORSE FROM THE OCEAN.` → `A BET ON ITS TAIL.` → `THE LOSER BECOMES A SLAVE.`

segments.voice: Kadru tells her snake sons: go and hang on the horse's tail, like black hairs, so I win. Some of them refuse. And Kadru, furious, curses the ones who refuse: they will burn in the fire of a snake sacrifice held by a king named Janamejaya. That's the line the whole frame hangs on. The fire we met on the first day was spoken over these snakes long before Janamejaya was born. And the text adds a hard detail. Brahma, the creator, hears the curse and lets it stand, because the snakes, the text says, had become fierce and poisonous, a danger to other creatures. So a mother's curse becomes part of a larger order. Then the bet plays out. The tail looks black, Vinata loses, and she becomes her sister's slave. The Adi Parva doesn't pretend any of this is simple. Kadru wins by a trick. And look who the curse falls on: not the cheat, but the sons who said no to cheating. The text doesn't explain that away or soften it. It leaves the unfairness on the page, with the creator's assent beside it, and lets the listener feel how uneasy that is. In Sanskrit, Janamejaya's rite is called the sarpasatra, the snake sacrifice, and its fire will come long afterward, lit by a king who thinks only of his father. And one more thread starts here. Vinata has a son still to come out of his egg, a great bird. He'll be the one to set her free.
screen: `HANG ON THE TAIL LIKE BLACK HAIRS.` · `A CURSE ON THE SONS WHO REFUSED.` · `BRAHMA LETS IT STAND.` · `VINATA LOSES, AND SERVES.` · then, large: `SARPASATRA: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let a few breaths pass. Bring to mind a time someone asked you to help them win by bending something: cover for them, shade a number, take their side before you knew the facts. Maybe you said yes. Maybe you said no, and it cost you. Don't grade either. Just remember how the asking felt in the body: the chest, the jaw, the hands. Breathe in, and feel that pull. Breathe out, and notice the room where a no can live. The bell holds the time.
